steps.prompt: Write the move you chose. Then name one reply by the other side that you did NOT test before you moved. Nothing is explained yet.

fields.label: A reply I did not test:

steps.text:
**This lesson, as four tests you can take yourself.**
1. **See** a fork, for every kind of piece.
2. **Check** it against the four answers an opponent can give.
3. **Set one up** with forcing moves.
4. **Stop** one against you, and teach it to a beginner.
A **fork** is one move that makes two threats. It wins only when no single reply meets both.

steps.title: Same jump, one change
steps.prompt: Black's king now stands on d8. Does the knight jump to the same square still win the queen? Predict first, then check.
What changed between the two positions, and why did it matter?

fields.label: What changed:
options: the king now covers the landing square
fields.answer: the king now covers the landing square

steps.caption: A third version: one more black piece. Step through the jump.

line.say: The knight lands on c7 and again attacks the king and the queen.
But the rook on c8 guards c7 and takes the knight. A fork needs a landing square that is safe.

claims.statement: One black piece, the rook on c8, attacks the landing square c7.
Along the engine line the knight jump nets no material.

steps.text: **How to look for it.** First, find the enemy pieces that are loose or valuable, and the king. Then look for one square that touches two of them, whatever piece could land there; a check is the strongest start. Last, ask whether your piece is safe on that square and whether one reply could meet both threats.

**The idea, with its conditions.** A fork is one move that attacks two targets at once. It usually wins material when the opponent has no single reply that deals with both; you will test four kinds of reply later. Check the landing square first, because a forker that is simply captured for nothing is a classic failure. [I] Znosko-Borovsky separated real from fictitious threats [V-sheet]; treating a fork as two threats and asking about each is my own use of that idea.

**[H] Which forks get missed?** Hypothesis, not finding: the knight fork is the one people miss most, because its jump leaves no line between it and its targets, and eyes look for lines. Our own puzzle bank cannot test this. [V, reviewer's recount] Among the 81 single-move fork puzzles in the bank (filter: fork theme, find the move), 30 start with a knight move and 24 with a queen move. That shows what the bank contains, not what players miss.

steps.caption: Knight map: from c7 the knight touches six squares, and two of them hold the black king and the rook.

line.say: The knight lands on c7, where its jumps reach both the king and the rook.
The king has to move, because it is in check.
Now the knight takes the rook. The check bought the time.

claims.statement: A knight on c7 attacks exactly these six squares.
The knight attacks the rook on a6.
The knight attacks the king on e8.
Along the engine line the jump wins at least a rook.

steps.caption: An endgame fork. White's pawn on b6 wants to run, and Black's rook stands on b3.

line.say: The knight checks the king on f5 and attacks the rook on b3 at once.
The king steps aside. Nothing defends the rook.
The knight takes the rook, and the b-pawn is free to advance.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the rook on b3.
The knight attacks the king on f5.
No black piece defends the rook on b3.
Along the engine line the jump wins the rook.

steps.caption: No check this time: a quiet knight jump. Black to move.

line.say: The knight lands where it attacks both the rook on d4 and the queen on f4.
The queen has to move.
The knight takes the rook.
The queen takes the knight. Black has won the exchange, not the queen.

claims.statement: A knight on e6 attacks exactly these squares.
Along the engine line the jump nets material.

steps.caption: Pawn map: a pawn attacks the two squares diagonally ahead of it. A pawn on d5 hits c6 and e6.

line.say: The pawn steps forward and attacks both knights.
One knight escapes.
The pawn takes the other one.
Black recaptures the pawn, but White has won a knight for a pawn.

claims.statement: A pawn on d5 attacks exactly c6 and e6.
Along the engine line the pawn move nets material.

steps.caption: A pawn fork, and what it sets up next. Black to move.

line.say: The pawn attacks the queen on e2 and the rook on c2.
White takes the pawn with the other rook.
The black queen now checks the king and attacks the rook on d3: a second fork.
White blocks with the queen.
Black takes the rook.

claims.statement: The pawn attacks the queen on e2.
The pawn attacks the rook on c2.
The queen on e4 attacks the king on g2.
The queen on e4 attacks the rook on d3.
Along the engine line the pawn move nets material.

steps.caption: A pawn check that forks the king and the queen. White to move.

line.say: The pawn checks the king on e6 and attacks the queen on g6.
If the queen takes the pawn, that also answers the check.
The rook takes the queen.
The king takes the rook. White gave a pawn and a rook for the queen.

claims.statement: The pawn attacks the queen on g6.
The pawn attacks the king on e6.

steps.caption: The queen forks from a distance. Black to move.

line.say: The queen checks the king along the diagonal and attacks the bishop on b2.
White interposes with the queen.
The queen takes the bishop.

claims.statement: The queen attacks the king on g1.
The queen attacks the bishop on b2.
Along the engine line the queen move nets material.

steps.caption: The queen forks along a diagonal and a file. White to move.

line.say: The queen checks along the diagonal and attacks the knight on d3 along the file.
The king steps aside.
The queen takes the knight.

claims.statement: The queen attacks the king on g8.
The queen attacks the knight on d3.
Along the engine line the queen move nets material.

steps.caption: A check from a distance, with a loose rook on the same diagonal. White to move.

line.say: The queen checks the king on h6 and attacks the rook on h2.
The king steps aside.
The queen takes the rook.

claims.statement: The queen attacks the king on h6.
The queen attacks the rook on h2.
Along the engine line the queen move nets material.

steps.caption: The bishop forks along its two diagonals: one to the king, one to a rook.

line.say: The bishop checks the king along one diagonal and attacks the rook on b3 along the other.
Black blocks the check with a pawn.
The bishop takes the rook.
The knight takes the bishop back.

claims.statement: The bishop attacks the king on g8.
The bishop attacks the rook on b3.
Along the engine line the bishop move nets material.

steps.caption: Count what can recapture before you rely on the check. Black to move.

line.say: The bishop checks the king and attacks the queen on a7.
White's queen may take the bishop.
But the rook on e5 takes the queen back. Black gave a bishop for a queen.

claims.statement: The bishop attacks the queen on a7.
One black piece guards the bishop on c5.
Along the engine line the bishop move nets material.

steps.caption: A rook forks along a rank by climbing to it. White to move.

line.say: The rook climbs the e-file and attacks both bishops along the fifth rank.
One bishop escapes.
The rook takes the other bishop.

claims.statement: The rook attacks the bishop on d5.
The rook attacks the bishop on g5.
Along the engine line the rook move nets material.

steps.caption: A rook check with a second target on the same rank, on the other side of the king.

line.say: The rook checks the king along the seventh rank and attacks the bishop on the other side.
The king steps out of check.
The rook takes the bishop.

claims.statement: The rook attacks the king on h7.
The rook attacks the bishop on b7.
Along the engine line the rook move nets material.

steps.caption: A king can fork too, when both pieces are loose and he does not step into a check.

line.say: The king steps up and attacks both the rook on d3 and the knight on d1.
The rook runs, but it still guards the knight along the file.
The white knight blocks that file, so the black knight loses its guard.
Black cannot save the knight.
The king takes it.

claims.statement: The king attacks the rook on d3.
The king attacks the knight on d1.
After the rook move, the rook on d4 still guards the knight on d1.
After the white knight blocks the file, nothing guards the knight on d1.
Along the engine line the king move nets material.

steps.text: **Remember.** A fork is one move that attacks two things at once. Look for a square that touches two targets, and ask whether your piece can land there safely. Any piece can fork, a check is the strongest kind, and it fails if the forker can simply be taken. Search: two targets, one square, a safe landing.
